before: When you go to a doctor, hospital, or specialist, you trust that the care you receive will help you — not make things worse. But sometimes a healthcare provider makes a mistake that causes serious harm: a misdiagnosis, a surgical error, a medication mix-up, or a failure to act on critical test results. If something feels wrong after medical treatment, you may be wondering: could this be medical malpractice, and what should I do about it? For a foundational overview of how these claims work, the Cornell Law Institute's medical malpractice summary provides useful context.

before:
• Do not confront the doctor or hospital about the mistake. While your instinct may be to demand answers, anything you say can be documented and potentially used against you later.
  • Do not provide a recorded statement to the provider's insurance company. Medical malpractice insurers will contact you early, often under the guise of "investigating the incident." Their goal is to gather information that can be used to deny or minimize your claim.
  • Do not sign any documents from the provider or insurer — including releases, waivers, or settlement offers — without having an attorney review them first.
  • Do not post details on social media. Defense attorneys routinely search patients' social media profiles for posts that can be used to dispute injury claims.
after:
• Do not confront the doctor or hospital about the mistake. While your instinct may be to demand answers, anything you say can be documented and potentially used against you later.
  • Do not provide a recorded statement to the provider's insurance company. The provider's malpractice insurer or the hospital's risk-management office may contact you, sometimes describing the call as an investigation of the incident. Anything you tell them can be used to evaluate — and contest — your claim.
  • Do not sign any documents from the provider or insurer — including releases, waivers, or settlement offers — without having an attorney review them first.
  • Do not post details on social media. Defense attorneys routinely search patients' social media profiles for posts that can be used to dispute injury claims.

before: In Georgia, you must file a sworn affidavit from a qualified medical expert simultaneously with your complaint. The expert must confirm that the provider deviated from the standard of care and that the deviation caused your injury. Filing without a proper affidavit results in dismissal. This means your attorney must retain an expert, obtain and review all records, and have the expert prepare a sworn statement — all before the lawsuit is filed.
after: In Georgia, you must file a sworn affidavit from a qualified medical expert simultaneously with your complaint. The expert must identify at least one specific negligent act or omission and the facts supporting it. Filing without the affidavit results in dismissal; a defective one can be fixed only by amending within 30 days of the defendant's motion (O.C.G.A. § 9-11-9.1(e)). This means your attorney must retain an expert, obtain and review all records, and have the expert prepare a sworn statement — all before the lawsuit is filed.

before:
• Misdiagnosis or delayed diagnosis — cancer, heart attack, stroke, or infection that was missed or diagnosed too late for effective treatment
  • Surgical errors — wrong-site surgery, nerve damage, organ perforation, or retained surgical instruments
  • Medication errors — wrong drug, wrong dosage, dangerous interactions, or allergic reactions that should have been anticipated
  • Birth injuries — cerebral palsy, Erb's palsy, brain damage, or other injuries during labor and delivery
  • Anesthesia errors — overdose, underdose, failure to monitor, or intubation injuries
  • Emergency room negligence — premature discharge, failure to order appropriate tests, or misreading results
  • Nursing home neglect — falls, bedsores, medication errors, malnutrition, or dehydration due to inadequate care
  • Failure to obtain informed consent — proceeding without explaining the risks, alternatives, and potential complications
  • Wrongful death — fatal medical errors where the patient's family may have a claim

before: If you suspect medical malpractice, act quickly: get independent medical care, request your complete records, document everything, and avoid discussing the situation with the provider or their insurer. Georgia requires a two-year filing and expert affidavit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71, § 9-11-9.1); South Carolina allows three years but requires a Notice of Intent to File Suit, filed together with a qualified expert's affidavit, and then mandatory mediation, before suit (S.C. Code § 15-3-545, § 15-79-125). Both states have strict statutes of repose — five years in Georgia, six in South Carolina.
after: If you suspect medical malpractice, act quickly: get independent medical care, request your complete records, document everything, and avoid discussing the situation with the provider or their insurer. Georgia requires suit within two years from the injury, filed with an expert affidavit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71, § 9-11-9.1); South Carolina allows three years but requires a Notice of Intent to File Suit, filed together with a qualified expert's affidavit, and then mandatory mediation, before suit (S.C. Code § 15-3-545, § 15-79-125). Both states have strict statutes of repose — five years in Georgia, six in South Carolina.
Suspect medical malpractice in Georgia or South Carolina? Get independent care, request your records, avoid the insurer, and act before strict deadlines.

before: Georgia imposes a two-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71) from the date the injury occurred. There is no general discovery rule: only a foreign object left in the body gets one year from discovery (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-72). An absolute five-year statute of repose applies. Georgia also requires an expert affidavit at the time of filing (O.C.G.A. § 9-11-9.1).
after: Georgia imposes a two-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71) from the date the injury occurred. There is no general discovery rule: only a foreign object left in the body gets one year from discovery (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-72). A five-year statute of repose applies to everything except foreign-object cases and children injured before age five, who have until their tenth birthday (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-73). Georgia also requires an expert affidavit at the time of filing (O.C.G.A. § 9-11-9.1).

before: South Carolina allows three years from the date of the negligent act or from discovery (S.C. Code § 15-3-545), with a six-year statute of repose. Before suing, you must also file a Notice of Intent to File Suit together with a qualified expert's affidavit, and serve it on each defendant, which tolls the deadline; the parties must then mediate before the lawsuit can be filed (S.C. Code §§ 15-79-125, 15-36-100).
after: South Carolina allows three years from the date of the negligent act or from discovery or when it reasonably ought to have been discovered (S.C. Code § 15-3-545), with a six-year statute of repose. Before suing, you must also file a Notice of Intent to File Suit together with a qualified expert's affidavit — filing it tolls the deadline — and serve it on each defendant; the parties must then mediate, within 90 to 120 days of service, before the lawsuit can be filed (S.C. Code §§ 15-79-125, 15-36-100).
